summary: Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol version 3 can tunnel a variety of data link protocols over IP networks. This document describes the specifics of tunneling High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC) frames over L2TPv3. It is standards-track and was updated by RFC 5641.

plainLanguage.summary: This document describes how to carry HDLC frames across an IP network using L2TPv3. The result is called an HDLC pseudowire, because the two ends behave as if one HDLC wire ran between them. It also defines how one end tells the other that the wire has come up or gone down.

subtitle: How to carry HDLC frames across an IP network as an L2TPv3 pseudowire, including link status signalling.

tldr.problem: Serial links that use HDLC framing need to be joined across an IP network as if the link were a single wire.
tldr.mechanism: Each HDLC interface is paired with an L2TPv3 session of pseudowire type 0x0006; frames lose their flags and FCS and cross the tunnel, and the Circuit Status AVP in Set Link Info messages reports whether the link is up.
tldr.outcome: Anything with HDLC-like framing, such as PPP, Frame Relay or X.25, can cross the tunnel, with the endpoints taking no part in those protocols. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 5641.

today: RFC 4349 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2006. It has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 5641. It builds on the base L2TPv3 protocol in RFC 3931.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3931 defines a base protocol for Layer 2 Tunneling over IP networks. This document defines the specifics necessary for tunneling HDLC frames over L2TPv3. Such emulated circuits are referred to as HDLC Pseudowires (HDLCPWs).

The protocol specifics defined here include those necessary for simple point-to-point frame encapsulation, for example between two L2TPv3 nodes, and for simple interface up and interface down notifications. The reader is expected to be very familiar with the terminology and protocol constructs defined in RFC 3931.

The abbreviations used throughout are HDLC (High-Level Data Link Control), HDLCPW (HDLC Pseudowire), LAC (L2TP Access Concentrator), LCCE (L2TP Control Connection Endpoint) and PW (Pseudowire).
sections.plainLanguage: This document describes how to carry HDLC frames across an IP network using L2TPv3. The result is called an HDLC pseudowire, because the two ends behave as if one HDLC wire ran between them. It also defines how one end tells the other that the wire has come up or gone down.

sections.title: Control Connection Establishment
sections.content:
To tunnel an HDLC link over IP using L2TPv3, an L2TPv3 control connection MUST first be established as described in RFC 3931. The SCCRQ and SCCRP control messages MUST include the HDLC Pseudowire Type of 0x0006 in the Pseudowire Capabilities List, which identifies the control connection as able to establish L2TP sessions that support HDLC pseudowires.

An LCCE MUST be able to identify itself uniquely in the SCCRQ and SCCRP messages via a globally unique value. By default this is advertised via the structured Router ID AVP, though the unstructured Hostname AVP MAY be used to identify LCCEs as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any HDLC frames can cross the network, the two endpoints set up an L2TPv3 control connection. Each one names the HDLC pseudowire type in that exchange, so both know the tunnel can carry this kind of wire.

sections.title: Session Establishment and Teardown
sections.content:
Associating an HDLC serial interface with a pseudowire, and its transition to ready or up, results in the establishment of an L2TP session via the standard three-way handshake described in Section 3.4.1 of RFC 3931. This document calls the local act of associating an interface running HDLC with a pseudowire provisioning the HDLC interface, and its transition to ready or up the interface becoming ACTIVE. The transition to not-ready or down is the interface becoming INACTIVE.

An LCCE MAY initiate the session immediately upon association with an HDLC interface, or wait until the interface becomes ACTIVE. Waiting until then may be preferred, as it delays allocation of resources until absolutely necessary. The Pseudowire Type AVP, Attribute Type 68, MUST be present in the ICRQ messages and MUST include the Pseudowire Type of 0x0006 for HDLCPWs. The Circuit Status AVP MUST be present in the ICRQ and ICRP messages and MAY be present in the SLI message.

The Remote End ID AVP MUST be present in the ICRQ, in order to identify the HDLC link with which to associate the L2TP session. It is of opaque form and variable length, though at a minimum an unstructured four-octet value known to both LCCEs must be supported, either by direct configuration or some other means. How that value is configured, retrieved, discovered or otherwise determined at each LCCE is outside the scope of this document.

If the far end has not been provisioned for the interface identified in the ICRQ, a CDN is returned immediately, indicating that the associated link was not provisioned or available at that LCCE. The initiator SHOULD then use a periodic retry mechanism, and the period and the maximum number of retries MUST be configurable. An implementation MAY send an ICRQ or ICRP before an HDLC interface is ACTIVE, as long as the Circuit Status AVP reflects that the link is INACTIVE and an SLI is sent when the HDLC interface becomes ACTIVE. The ICCN is the final stage in the session establishment, confirming the receipt of the ICRP with acceptable parameters to allow bidirectional traffic.

In the event a link is removed at either LCCE, the associated L2TP session MUST be torn down via the CDN message. Two additional HDLC result codes are defined for that message: 20, the HDLC link was deleted permanently and is no longer provisioned, and 21, the HDLC link has been INACTIVE for an extended period of time.
sections.plainLanguage: When each end of the HDLC wire is ready, the two endpoints exchange three short messages: a request, a reply and a confirmation. That handshake opens the tunnel for traffic in both directions. If the far end has no such wire configured, it refuses the request, and the initiating end retries on a timer the operator can set.

sections.title: Link Status Notification and the Circuit Status AVP
sections.content:
HDLC pseudowires use the Set Link Info (SLI) control message defined in RFC 3931 to signal HDLC link status notifications between the two ends. The SLI message is a single message that is sent over the L2TP control channel, signalling the interface state change. It MUST be sent any time there is a status change of any values identified in the Circuit Status AVP. The only exceptions are the initial ICRQ, ICRP and CDN messages, which establish and tear down the L2TP session itself. The SLI message may be sent from either end at any time after the first ICRQ is sent, and perhaps before an ICRP is received, which then requires the peer to perform a reverse Session ID lookup.

All sessions established by a given control connection use the L2TP Hello facility for session keepalive. This gives all sessions basic dead peer and path detection between the endpoints.

HDLC reports Circuit Status with the Circuit Status AVP defined in RFC 3931, Attribute Type 71. Its value is a 16-bit mask with the two least significant bits defined and the remaining bits reserved for future use. Reserved bits MUST be set to 0 when sending and ignored upon receipt. The N (New) bit SHOULD be set to one if the Circuit Status indication is for a new HDLC circuit, and to zero otherwise. The A (Active) bit indicates whether the HDLC interface is ACTIVE (1) or INACTIVE (0). In the example exchange in the RFC, an active new link is reported with a status of 0x03.
sections.plainLanguage: When the wire at one end comes up or goes down, that end sends a short notice to the other over the control channel. The notice carries a 16-bit value in which only two bits are defined: one says the circuit is new, the other says the interface is working. Both ends also exchange periodic hello messages, so each can tell whether the other is still there.

sections.title: Data Packet Encapsulation
sections.content:
HDLCPWs use the default encapsulations defined in RFC 3931 for demultiplexing, sequencing and flags. The type is intended to operate in an interface-to-interface or port-to-port fashion, passing all HDLC data and control PDUs over the pseudowire. The HDLC PDU is stripped of flags and trailing FCS, bit or byte unstuffing is performed, and the remaining data, including the address, control and protocol fields, is transported over the pseudowire.

Since all packets are passed in a largely transparent manner over the HDLCPW, any protocol that has HDLC-like framing may use the HDLCPW mode, including PPP, Frame Relay (port-to-port Frame Relay transport) and X.25 (LAPB). In such cases, the negotiations and signalling of the specific protocols transported over the HDLCPW take place between the remote systems, and the LCCEs do not take part in them.

  • When the HDLCPW transports Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) traffic, PPP negotiations (Link Control Protocol, optional authentication and Network Control Protocols) are performed between the remote systems, and the LCCEs do not participate.
  • When the HDLCPW transports Frame Relay traffic, PVC status management procedures (Local Management Interface) take place between the remote systems, and the LCCEs do not participate in LMI. Individual Frame Relay virtual circuits are not visible to the LCCEs, and the FECN, BECN and DE bits are transported transparently.
  • When the HDLCPW transports X.25 (LAPB) traffic, the LCCEs do not function as either LAPB DCE or DTE devices.

Exceptions include cases where direct access to the HDLC interface is required, or modes that operate on the flags, FCS, or bit and byte unstuffing that is performed before the HDLC PDU is sent over the pseudowire. PPP ACCM negotiation is given as an example.

Data packet sequencing MAY be enabled for HDLCPWs, using the sequencing mechanisms of RFC 3931. When sequencing is enabled, HDLCPWs MUST request the presence of the L2TPv3 Default L2-Specific Sublayer, and MAY request its presence at all times.
sections.plainLanguage: Each HDLC frame is stripped of its start and end markers and its error check, and the remaining bytes are carried inside an L2TPv3 packet and rebuilt into a frame at the far end. Because the middle is transparent, protocols that use the same kind of framing, such as PPP, Frame Relay and X.25, can be carried the same way. The two real systems talk to each other directly, and the tunnel endpoints take no part in their negotiations.

sections.title: MTU Considerations
sections.content:
With L2TPv3 as the tunneling protocol, the packet resulting from the encapsulation is N bytes longer than the HDLC frame without the flags or FCS. The value of N depends on the following fields.

  • L2TP session header: Flags, Ver and Res take 4 octets, when L2TPv3 runs over UDP only; the Session ID takes 4 octets; the Cookie Size is 0, 4 or 8 octets.
  • L2-Specific Sublayer: 0 or 4 octets, that is, when sequencing is used.

The resulting ranges for N in octets are 4 to 16 when the L2TPv3 data messages are over IP, and 16 to 28 when they are over UDP. N does not include the IP header. The MTU and fragmentation implications resulting from this are discussed in Section 4.1.4 of RFC 3931.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tunneled packet is bigger than the frame it carries. Over IP the extra room is 4 to 16 bytes, and over UDP it is 16 to 28 bytes, not counting the IP header. That extra size can matter when a path cannot carry a large packet.

sections.title: Applicability Statement
sections.content:
HDLC pseudowires support a port-to-port or interface-to-interface deployment model operating in a point-to-point fashion. In addition to the transport of HDLC frames, a natural application of HDLCPWs allows for the transport of any protocol using an HDLC-like framing.

The HDLCPW emulation over a packet-switched network has the following characteristics in relationship to the native service.

  • HDLC data and control fields are transported transparently. The specific negotiations and signalling of the protocol being transported are performed between the remote systems, and the LCCE does not participate in them.
  • The trailing FCS, which contains a CRC, is stripped at the ingress LCCE and is not transported over the HDLCPW. It is therefore regenerated at the egress LCCE. This means that the FCS may not accurately reflect errors on the end-to-end HDLC link, and errors or corruption introduced in the HDLCPW payload during encapsulation or transit across the packet-switched network may not be detected. This may not be of concern if the inner payloads or upper protocols transported perform their own error and integrity checking. To allow for payload integrity-checking transparency on HDLCPWs using L2TP over IP or L2TP over UDP/IP, the L2TPv3 session can utilize IPsec.
  • HDLC link status notification is provided using the Circuit Status AVP in the SLI message.
  • The length of the resulting L2TPv3 packet is longer than the encapsulated HDLC frame without flags and FCS, with the resulting MTU and fragmentation implications.
  • The packet-switched network may reorder, duplicate or silently drop packets. Sequencing may be enabled in the HDLCPW for some or all packets to detect lost, duplicate or out-of-order packets on a per-session basis.
  • The faithfulness of an HDLCPW may be increased by leveraging Quality of Service features of the LCCEs and the underlying packet-switched network.
sections.plainLanguage: The pseudowire behaves like the native wire in most ways, but two things differ. The error check is removed at one end and rebuilt at the other, so damage in the middle may go unnoticed unless the protocols inside check for themselves. The network in between may also reorder or drop packets, which per-session sequencing can detect.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: HDLC over L2TPv3 is subject to the security considerations defined in RFC 3931. Beyond the considerations when carrying other data link types, there are no additional considerations specific to carrying HDLC.
sections.plainLanguage: The same security rules apply as for the base tunnel protocol. This document adds no rules of its own for carrying HDLC.
